asr.full_text: So how do you really handle a tech support call when you're not very tech savvy? That's what we're going to talk about in this video. Hi there, ninja! Welcome back again. My name is Rhea and you're still watching Call Center Ninja. If you're new here, I'm sharing real stories and tips to help you start, enjoy, and survive your call center lifestyle. So please consider subscribing. Just click the red subscribe button below. And you're so much if you've already subscribed. So let's just say that you really want to apply for a call center job but you're worried because you're not very tech savvy. So you're considering whether a call center job is the right job for you or not. But let me thank you that you can still apply for a job account for a tech support center even though you're not really tech savvy. If you remember, I mentioned in my previous videos that I was profiled for a banking and financial account when I had no idea about banking and financial stuff right before I applied for a call center job. But because there was training involved before you actually got to take calls, you'll still be equipped even if you don't have any experience at all. So, one of our viewers requested this video. How do you become a tech support specialist when you don't have any computer science or IT background at all? Well, you don't have to worry because apart from the training that will be provided by your company or by your account, everything can actually be learned. And in a tech support account based on customer service, it will usually only be the basic stuff if you're a frontline person. So, you're not really going to dig into the more complicated part unless you get promoted to another skill or another level of tech support where you take escalations. But even then, you're still going to be trained for that. My tip number one is to be open for learning. First and foremost, when you're in a tech support account or when you're profiled for that type of account. You might think that I might not be able to do this because I'm not very tech savvy. You don't have that kind of mindset. You have to be open for learning or for new things. So even if you're not very tech savvy. But as long as you know how to learn and you're open for learning. You know how to use a computer. You at least know how to turn on or turn on a computer and navigate. Then you shouldn't have any problem. And in fact, if you're watching this video right now, then you should be able to turn off the computer. Then that means you were able to go to YouTube, you were able to log in, you were able to access the internet using your phone or your computer, then that means that you have at least, even just a little bit of knowledge about computers and about the internet. The rest of the things, you will learn during your training. So don't close your mind to learning. Everything can be learned. Tip number two, this is a cliche or it might always sound a cliche because I say this. But for every skill you have to learn, you really just need to practice and learn it. For the consumer tech industry, a lot of the concerns are about software, hardware, applications, internet, troubleshooting. So when you get there, when you're already trained for it, make sure that you take some time to practice your tools. And because you're going to be using those tools every day of your life as you work, those are the only tools that are important to you right now. You don't really have to get distracted with so many things at once. Just practice the tools that you're allowed to use. So number one is your navigation skills. When I was a trainer, I used to have a navigation test for my trainees. So what would usually happen is I ask them to master the different tools and the different links. Like where to go, for example, if they needed to change the password for online banking, where to go if they needed to change the address, if they needed to help a customer with browser troubleshooting. So I would ask them, okay, for example, Ben, where do you go on your tool to access the password reset for your customer? So that trainee would have to look for it on his own and tell me where he or she can find it. So that way, with navigation testing, you don't really have to worry about assisting the customer yet. But you're focusing on how to use the tool first and how to master it. Now, every tool that you're supposed to use and you're allowed to use should be mastered. Because that will also help with your efficiency as a tech support specialist. And once you master the tool, this includes your knowledge base and your job aids. Once you master those, then it will be easier for you to provide resolution as a tech support specialist. And I'm telling you, even though you don't really have that much experience with tech support industry, that's not really a problem. So let's just say you already have an open mind for learning. So let's just say you've already mastered or at least you're learning how to master your navigation tools. Or your knowledge base or your drawbacks. You have a great idea of how to handle the computer and everything that goes with it. Then you now have to think about how you're going to handle that tech support call. So the third tip in relation to that is going to be to identify the problem or the issue right at the beginning of the call. So, of course, after you've empathised your greeting or apologized, then you need to start identifying the problem. So how do you identify the problem? It's just really the same with all the other types of calls. But with tech support calls, what I would usually like to start with is, what is the error message? Or what is the problem, the specific problem that the customer encounters? For example, in online banking, if the customer says, I can't log into my account on your website. So the problem is that the customer can't log into the website. But then I had to know how to solve that problem. So the very first question I would ask is, what is or what was the error message that you're seeing? Or what can you see on your screen right now? Can you please tell me what you can see on your screen right now? Or if it's not an internet issue, you can ask your customer. Can you please describe to me what you did before that resulted in that call? Or if the customer doesn't know that at all, then you have to be descriptive with your question. So it really has to be the right question so that you get the right answer from your customer. Another thing is that you can always check existing or previous tickets or previous issues. Issues that might have already been resolved by your colleagues or by other specialists or representatives. You already have the solution ready for the customer. Tip number four is to evaluate your customer's technical level or skill level without actually discriminating or looking down on the customer. Because although for you as a tech support specialist, the issue may be very, very simple, but it may not be for your customer. And you have to understand that different customers have different needs. Some customers find it really easy to fix and can really follow your simple instructions. Some customers may find it difficult to follow your instructions. It could be because of the way you deliver the instructions or it's just that the customer isn't very used to technology or computers that she needs more help navigating her computer or his software. So, in this case, once you've evaluated the customer's technical skill, that's how you'll know, how you'll respond to the customer and how you'll provide the instructions. So if you measure that the customer is a fast learner or basically knows how to navigate the computer, then at least you can just provide the instructions easily. So it'll save you some time. You don't really have to go very specific about it. But if you know that the customer is having a hard time understanding the tech behind it, then I would always advise you to be very descriptive and specific with your instructions. In fact, I always tell my trainees this, to be considerate of the customers because again, they have different levels of savviness. So if you feel that your customer is a little behind in the tech part, be involved with your descriptive step-by-step instructions. So if possible, you can tell the customer, Mr. Customer first, we have to close the browser window, just click the X button at the top. You have to be really descriptive like that, even for the callers. The customer says, I don't know which browser I'm using. So you have to explain it in layman's terms. Are you using Mozilla Firefox? Are you using Google Chrome? You give them options to make it easier for them to understand. If the customer doesn't understand Mozilla Firefox or Google Chrome, ask them. Are you seeing an orange icon? Like a fire icon? Are you seeing a blue, green, red icon? So try to be descriptive for them. Adjust to their needs because they are the customers and you should be the one adjusting for them. And my tip number five is to have a lot of patience. Not to get your customers impatient, but also to get yourself impatient. Because sometimes with these types of calls, you just get to be patient. With tech support, it's highly likely that your handling time is much higher or longer. Because of the fact that sometimes you need to be on the line with the customer. Until the issue is resolved. Or let's say until the customer is able to connect to the internet. Or is able to log into the website. Because you don't want customers who keep calling for the same issues over and over. You'd want to solve it in that one specific hall. So that's about it for today. I hope you've learned something from this video. And as usual, if you like this content, please like, subscribe if you haven't yet. And remember, I have videos every Wednesday and Friday. So see you again next time. Take care and bye-bye!
